video_title: Real Estate To Drop 30%, Stocks To Fall 50%? | Michael Pento
gist: Michael Pento argues the US is in the terminal phase of a first-ever-concurrent equity/credit/real-estate 'triple bubble' fed by Fed money-printing and record debt, and predicts stocks fall 50%+ and real estate 25-30% in an eventual deflationary depression (possibly 2027) followed by unprecedented hyper-stagflation once the government is forced to monetize the response — while war-driven yen/oil dynamics, new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's balance-sheet fight, and cracking AI-mania valuations (via collapsing Chinese compute prices) are the near-term catalysts to watch.

themes.theme: Five-Sector Cycle Model and Current Positioning

insights.claim: Michael Pento runs a proprietary five-sector business-cycle model (deflation, disinflation, stasis/neutral, reflation, hyper-stagflation/hyperinflation) with a different portfolio allocation for each sector, and currently has the portfolio parked in Sector 3 (stasis).
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gives investors a concrete regime-based allocation framework to track rather than a single static call; watch for Pento announcing a sector shift as a signal.

insights.claim: With markets whipsawing on Iran headlines, Pento has neutralized his portfolio into Sector 3: mostly equal-weight S&P 500, some inflation-protection assets, some disinflation-protection assets, a modest gold position, and hedges, rather than making a directional bet.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Signals that even a bear-case macro strategist is choosing not to make an aggressive directional bet right now given headline-driven volatility — a case for staying flexible rather than pressing a single thesis.
insights.quote: I've just gone mostly heavy in equal weight S&P 500. I have some inflationary components to the model to to the portfolio.

insights.claim: Since the US went to war with Iran on February 28, Pento's business-cycle model has compressed from moving over months/years to flipping in a matter of weeks or even days, driven by news-cycle mood swings between the IRGC and the White House.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Model-based investors should expect faster, noisier regime signals right now and size positions accordingly rather than assuming normal multi-month cycle durations.
insights.quote: since February 28th, the cycles have been very compressed and they've they become a matter of weeks and even days sometimes

insights.claim: Pento's gold position is currently modest (not overweight) because gold has been struggling against rising real interest rates, but he plans to substantially increase gold and gold-miner exposure once evidence of an economic slowdown appears.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gold allocation is a trigger-based trade for Pento tied to slowdown confirmation, not a current core overweight — investors following his framework should watch growth data, not just inflation, before adding gold.
insights.quote: We have some gold, not overweight gold because gold does not like rising interest rates and interest rates have been rising especially in real terms.

insights.claim: Pushed for a directional lean, Pento says he is leaning slightly toward the path from Sector 3 into disinflation/deflation/recession (Sector 1) rather than back into reflation, based on five-year inflation expectations having come down significantly — but he explicitly warns that a renewed Iran/oil shock would invalidate that lean.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: His base case favors deflationary assets over inflation hedges near-term, but the position is explicitly conditional on the Iran conflict not re-escalating — a clear risk trigger to monitor.
insights.quote: if you push the issue with me, I would say I'm leaning slightly on the disinflation heading towards deflation and recession path.

themes.theme: Iran War, Yen Mechanics, and the Bond-Yield Transmission Channel

insights.claim: Pento traces a direct causal chain from the Iran conflict to US bond yields: Japan must sell yen to buy dollars to pay for oil (priced in dollars), and as oil prices spike this selling accelerates, weakening the yen faster and forcing the Bank of Japan — the largest foreign holder of Treasuries — to sell Treasuries to support the yen, which pushes US yields even higher.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A non-obvious transmission mechanism linking Middle East oil shocks directly to the US long end of the curve — watch yen weakness and BOJ Treasury holdings as an early-warning gauge for US yield spikes.
insights.quote: which then causes the Bank of Japan to sell treasuries, the largest holder of treasuries, which sends yields even higher here in the United States.

insights.claim: Over the past few days the US has reportedly been selling euros to buy yen to prop up the yen and relieve pressure on Treasury yields — Pento calls this a short-term band-aid, arguing the real fix is getting energy prices down so the BOJ doesn't need to keep dumping Treasuries.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: FX intervention is being used as a stopgap for bond-market stress; if oil doesn't come down, this band-aid runs out and yield pressure resumes.
insights.quote: And that's a very short-term band-aid. Very short term. I mean how many euros do we have to sell to to buy yen?

insights.claim: Pento reads a recurring political pattern: whenever 30-year yields climb toward 5% and WTI oil approaches $90, the administration suddenly signals a deal is close on Iran, because spiking yields and gas prices are 'political kryptonite' heading into the midterms.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Frames Iran de-escalation headlines as a function of bond/oil market pain thresholds rather than diplomacy — a tradeable pattern for anticipating headline-driven reversals in yields and oil.
insights.quote: once yields start climbing, you know, well above 5% on the 30 year and oil prices tick toward back towards 90 on WTI, all of a sudden we have a deal.

insights.claim: Pento believes without the Iran conflict oil and commodity prices would be materially lower and the US would not have added an incremental roughly $1.5 trillion in national-defense spending onto the debt pile, which itself pressures Treasury supply and yields.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Quantifies the fiscal cost side of the war as an additional yield-pressure input independent of the oil-price channel.

insights.claim: Pento's strong personal opinion is that Trump does not want two years as a lame-duck president facing investigations after the midterms, so he is managing the Iran conflict's intensity around the election calendar and will likely push harder — including occupying western Iran to keep the Strait of Hormuz open — only after the midterms are past.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Suggests investors should expect Iran-driven volatility to be actively managed down through the midterms and then potentially escalate afterward, affecting the timing of oil/yield spikes.
insights.quote: he doesn't want two more years two years of a lame duck presidency which is going to be riddled with investigations.

insights.claim: Pento does not expect the bottom 80% of the population to see real relief from inflation before the midterms; he expects headline inflation — which fell from 4.2% to 3.5% — to creep back up to the mid-to-upper 3% range at the next print.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Sets a near-term inflation floor expectation (mid-to-upper 3s) that argues against a pre-election disinflation narrative playing out for consumers.
insights.quote: I think it creeps back to the, you know, you know, mid to upper upper threes and the next inflation print.

themes.theme: Fed Policy Under Kevin Warsh: Balance Sheet and the Inflation Fight

insights.claim: Despite new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish inflation rhetoric since taking office (Pento cites May 22 as the start date), the Fed's balance sheet has actually grown by $38 billion since he took over — effectively a small dose of QE rather than the tightening his words imply.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A hawkish-sounding Fed chair is not yet backing words with balance-sheet action — a divergence worth tracking between Fed rhetoric and actual reserve/balance-sheet data.
insights.quote: the balance sheet, which he knows has to be reduced to get inflation under control, has actually grown by $ 38 billion. So he's almost in a form of QE right now.

insights.claim: The Fed's balance sheet was $800 billion before the Great Recession, ballooned to $9 trillion, was $4.5 trillion when Jerome Powell took office, and now sits just below $7 trillion — Pento argues it needs to shrink dramatically, back toward a 'scarce reserve regime,' to actually get inflation under control.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gives investors the specific balance-sheet levels to benchmark against for judging whether the Fed is genuinely tightening.

insights.claim: Bank reserves in the system, once negligible before a few years ago, are now above $3 trillion and earning interest paid by the Fed to banks — Pento calls this wasteful and argues reserves must be reduced to genuinely fight inflation.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Identifies excess bank reserves (not the fed funds rate) as the mechanism Pento believes actually drives inflation, reframing what 'real tightening' would require.

insights.claim: Pento predicts Warsh's planned 2027 task force/symposium on the balance sheet is really political cover: it lets Warsh blame a committee rather than himself when he finally announces balance-sheet shrinkage, after inflation has stayed above the Fed's 2% target for over five years.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Investors should treat the task force outcome as a likely pretext for a policy move already decided, not a genuine open deliberation.

insights.claim: Pento is confident Warsh genuinely intends to shrink the balance sheet given his Austrian-economics background, but predicts the attempt will only last a few months before the repo market and commercial paper freeze up, borrowing costs spike, and the Fed is forced to reverse course — with worse dynamics than prior taper attempts given today's higher debt and leverage levels.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A concrete falsifiable forecast: watch for repo-market and commercial-paper stress a few months into any real balance-sheet reduction as the signal the Fed is about to reverse.
insights.quote: maybe it lasts for a few months, the repo market freezes, commercial paper freezes, and that's when you know all heck breaks.

insights.claim: Pento argues the Fed's mandate has quietly morphed from lender-of-last-resort and price stability into an unstated rule of never allowing a recession, an uptick in unemployment, or even a stock-market pullback — a dynamic he says makes the eventual reckoning larger.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Frames Fed behavior as asset-price protection rather than price stability, implying markets are conditioned to expect Fed puts that Pento thinks will eventually fail.
insights.quote: Thou shalt never have a recession and thou shalt never have an uptick in the unemployment rate and thou shalt never have a bare market or even a pothole or a sinkhole in stock prices.

insights.claim: Pento sizes today's credit bubble at roughly $1.6 trillion in private credit, $1.4 trillion in collateralized loan obligations (CLOs), and $1.5 trillion in junk bonds.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Quantifies the size of the private-credit/leveraged-loan complex that would be exposed if the Fed shrinks reserves and credit conditions tighten.
insights.quote: You're talking about $1.6 trillion in private credit, $1.4 trillion in collateralized loan obligations, um $1.5 trillion in junk bonds.

insights.claim: Citing Morgan Stanley's estimate, Pento notes over $570 billion in AI-related debt is projected to be raised in 2026, with roughly $1 trillion estimated for 2027 — a rapidly growing new source of debt supply layered on top of existing credit-market stress.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: AI capex financing is becoming a material new competitor for capital in credit markets, adding to crowding-out pressure on yields.
insights.quote: There's going to be over half a trillion dollars 570 billion dollars in AI related debt raised in 2026.

insights.claim: US national debt stands at $40 trillion, or 123% of GDP and 720% of federal revenue, versus roughly 60% debt-to-GDP heading into the last two major recessions — Pento argues this leaves the government's balance sheet too broken to cushion the next downturn the way it did in 2001 and 2008.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A much higher debt-to-GDP starting point than prior cycles implies less fiscal/monetary headroom to absorb the next recession without a bond-market backlash.
insights.quote: that's 40 trillion 123% of GDP. That that amount of debt is 720% of our revenue.

insights.claim: The US is currently paying about $24 billion per week — over $1.2 trillion annually — in interest on the national debt, and Pento stresses this is happening 'in the good times,' before any recession-driven deficit blowout.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Establishes a baseline interest burden that will worsen sharply once rates and/or deficits rise further in a downturn, squeezing fiscal flexibility.
insights.quote: The interest that we pay on our national debt is $24 billion a week. We're paying over $1.2 trillion just in interest.

insights.claim: Pento expects annual deficits to roughly triple to about $6 trillion once the next recession hits, based on automatic stabilizers (unemployment insurance, SNAP, falling tax revenue) tripling deficits in the last two recessions — before any discretionary stimulus like TARP or universal-basic-income-style checks.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gives a specific quantitative deficit target ($6T) investors can use to model the fiscal/monetary response to the next downturn and its inflationary consequences.

insights.claim: Pento identifies the bond vigilantes' selling as driven by crowding out from a growing pile of AI-related debt competing with roughly $11 trillion in government debt that needs to be rolled over, with the Bank of Japan's Treasury sales acting as the immediate catalyst.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Identifies a structural supply/demand imbalance in Treasuries (debt rollover + AI debt issuance vs. shrinking foreign buyer support) as a persistent upward pressure on yields independent of the Iran conflict.

themes.theme: Triple Bubble Thesis and Price-Drop Targets

insights.claim: Pento says this is the first time in history that an equity bubble, a credit bubble, and a real estate bubble all exist concurrently, and each one is individually at record proportions rather than merely elevated.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: The core macro bear thesis: simultaneous record bubbles across three major asset classes raises the systemic severity of any unwind versus prior single-bubble cycles (dot-com, 2008 housing).
insights.quote: it's the first time in history concurrently you have an equity bubble, a credit bubble and a real estate bubble.

insights.claim: Total US equity market capitalization stands at 230% of GDP, about 130 percentage points above its long-term average, and the S&P 500's price-to-sales ratio is 70% above its long-term average.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Provides the two specific valuation metrics (market-cap/GDP and price/sales) Pento uses as his benchmark for how far equities would need to fall to reach historical norms.
insights.quote: you don't get total market cap of equities as a percentage of GDP to be 230% by osmosis

insights.claim: NYSE margin debt has hit an all-time record high of $1.5 trillion, an all-time record as a percentage of GDP, and is up 50% year-over-year — evidence for Pento that leverage-fueled speculation, not fundamentals, is driving equity gains.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Record margin debt is a classic late-cycle speculative excess indicator and a vulnerability if a deleveraging cascade begins.
insights.quote: We have we have $1.5 trillion dollar in margin debt. That's an all-time record high percent.

insights.claim: Pento's model shows real estate needs to fall roughly 25-30% to bring the home price-to-income ratio back to where it should be.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gives a specific, testable price target for the housing correction he expects, useful for gauging real estate exposure and timing.
insights.quote: Between 25 and 30% that would bring the home price to income ratio close to where it should be.

insights.claim: Pento says the stock market needs a drop of 'north of 50%' to bring valuation metrics like total-market-cap-to-GDP and price-to-sales back to historical norms, and cites the 2007-08 crisis — where the market fell 50% and took five years to regain its prior high — as the relevant precedent.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: The episode's headline call, explicitly quantified and anchored to a historical analog, giving investors a concrete downside scenario and recovery-timeline expectation to plan around.
insights.quote: you need something north of 50% to bring it back just to bring it back to historical metrics historical normal

themes.theme: The Deflationary Depression Call and Its Hyper-Stagflationary Aftermath

insights.claim: Pento's headline call is explicitly a 'depression,' not a recession — he argues the current reflation/disinflation 'carnival ride' ultimately ends in disinflation, then deflation, then depression, and says he can build the case for it across the interview.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Sets the framing for the entire interview: this is a depression call, a materially more severe outcome than a garden-variety recession, which should calibrate position sizing for tail-risk hedges.
insights.quote: I think it ends in disinflation then deflation and depression and I said D and I meant it it's depression not recession

insights.claim: Pento estimates the deflationary depression could arrive as early as 2027, contingent on how and when Fed Chair Kevin Warsh acts on the balance sheet.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Gives investors a rough timing anchor (2027) for the depression call, tied to a specific, observable trigger (Warsh's balance-sheet decision) rather than an open-ended forecast.
insights.quote: That's the deflationary depression which I think it could come in 2027 depending on what worsh does with the balance sheet.

insights.claim: Pento's expected sequence: either Warsh's balance-sheet shrinkage or a bond-market-forced yield spike pops the triple bubble, triggering bank failures and a violent unemployment spike; the fiscal/monetary response — automatic stabilizers plus likely TARP-style or UBI-style stimulus, financed by the Fed monetizing trillions more debt — then produces 'hyper stagflation like we have never seen before,' with the balance sheet potentially expanding from $7 trillion into the double digits.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Maps the full multi-stage scenario — crash, fiscal blowout, renewed money-printing, hyperstagflation — giving investors a roadmap of catalysts to watch in sequence rather than a single event.
insights.quote: I'm looking for to be specific hyper stagflation like we have never seen before as a direct necessity and a direct result of the fiscal and monetary policy

insights.claim: Citing NYU Stern data, Pento notes three historical 'lost decade' precedents for stocks: 0.6% average annual nominal return over the 20 years following the Great Depression, 0.5% over the 15-year 1969-1984 stagflation era, and 0.8% over the 12 years from 2000-2012 (the dot-com bubble unwind) — and argues today's valuations are more stretched than in any of those three periods, implying a comparable or worse lost decade is ahead, with real (inflation-adjusted) returns even worse than the nominal figures.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Provides historical base rates for what a 'lost decade' actually looks like in annualized terms, useful for setting realistic long-horizon return expectations if the bear case plays out.
insights.quote: In the 15 years of the stagflationary uh era from 69 to 84, it was 0.5%.

insights.claim: Pento predicts a 'huge return to active management' as the passive, buy-and-hold, target-date-fund approach that has dominated this cycle underperforms badly in a violent, compressed inflation/deflation cycle — he notes passive investors tend to get shaken out at the lows, making their realized returns worse than the already-poor buy-and-hold average.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A direct, if self-interested (Pento runs an active long/short strategy), call that passive index/target-date investors are structurally mispositioned for the volatility regime he expects.
insights.quote: I predict a huge return to active management.

themes.theme: K-Shaped Economy, Inflation as a Regressive Tax, and Early Labor Cracks

insights.claim: Both host and guest agree the current economy is, in aggregate, not the worst on record — unemployment is near record lows, ISM manufacturing came in at 55, and initial jobless claims are running around a historically low 200,000 per week — but a large cohort within the bottom 80% of earners is genuinely struggling because their wages, Social Security increases, and benefits are not keeping pace with inflation.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Distinguishes aggregate economic health (still fine) from the bifurcated reality households actually experience — important context before extrapolating recession/depression fears from consumer sentiment data alone.
insights.quote: in aggregate this is not the worst economy we has ever have ever seen. Not not even close in close.

insights.claim: Pento calls inflation 'the most regressive tax out there' because the bottom 80% spend a much larger share of income on energy, heating, cooling, food, and medicine, and lack the multiple homes and large investment portfolios that let the wealthy benefit from inflation-driven asset appreciation.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Frames inflation itself, not just recession risk, as the primary driver of the K-shaped wealth divide — relevant to how policy responses (rate cuts vs. balance-sheet action) will be judged politically.
insights.quote: Inflation is the tax. It's the most regressive tax out there.

insights.claim: Pento argues that if his deflationary-depression scenario plays out, it will not meaningfully help the bottom 80% even though it would shrink the wealth gap — the gap narrows only because it drags the top 20%'s asset wealth down (via crashing equities and real estate), not because the bottom cohort's situation improves; mass layoffs and bank failures would in fact make things worse for them before any 'clean slate' recovery two-to-three years later.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Warns against reading a coming crash as good news for lower-income households — the near-term pain (job losses, bank failures) hits them hardest even as it mechanically compresses the wealth gap.

insights.claim: Pento points to the household survey component of the June non-farm payrolls report showing a loss of 57,000 jobs, and 1.7 million jobs lost year-to-date in 2026 — noting the household survey historically leads the (more widely watched) establishment survey.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: A concrete, already-visible leading labor-market data point supporting Pento's view that the economy is slowing meaningfully in H2, ahead of it showing up in the headline establishment payrolls number.
insights.quote: In June, the household survey showed that we lost 57,000 jobs. And in the year so far, 2026, we lost 1.7 million jobs in the household survey.

insights.claim: Host Adam Taggart argues explicitly, and Pento agrees, that however painful the current economy feels for struggling households, a deflationary depression with mass job losses and bank failures would be materially worse — both frame this as a reason for people to take defensive financial steps now (protecting savings/income, planning for potential job loss) while unemployment is still low and markets are still near highs.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A direct actionable takeaway for viewers: use the current relatively benign labor market as the window to build financial resilience before Pento's downside scenario potentially arrives.

themes.theme: AI Mania: Cooling Signals and the Compute-Price Collapse

insights.claim: Pento sees the South Korean stock market — dominated by a couple of AI/semiconductor-linked names — falling roughly 40% in a handful of trading days as a red flag that something significant is breaking in the AI trade, alongside the SMH semiconductor ETF appearing to have peaked after hyperscalers had already cooled off.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Concrete, checkable market signals (SMH price action, Korean market drawdown) investors can monitor as early warnings that the AI trade's momentum leg is breaking down.
insights.quote: when I see the South Korean stock market go down 40% in a handful of trading days, that that gives you pause. Something really big is going on here.

insights.claim: Host Adam Taggart cites new pricing data showing AI compute costs collapsing: DeepSeek's V4 Flash costs about 3 cents to run a standard benchmark suite versus 86 cents for Moonshot AI's Kimi K3, $1.86 for OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sohu, and $3.15 for Anthropic's Claude Fable 5 (the industry's top-scoring model) — making the cheapest Chinese model over 100x cheaper than the leading American flagship.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: A sharply falling cost curve for AI inference, led by Chinese models, directly threatens the revenue/margin assumptions embedded in hyperscaler and AI-infrastructure valuations.
insights.quote: In realized terms, the Chinese model is more than a hundred times cheaper to run than the American flagship.

insights.claim: Adam Taggart notes reports that large firms like Microsoft are increasingly routing the bulk of their AI workloads to cheaper Chinese models, reserving premium US models only for the highest-end tasks — which he argues threatens the profit forecasts analysts currently have built into hyperscaler and AI-player valuations.
insights.speaker: Adam Taggart
insights.so_what: If enterprise buyers commoditize the bulk of inference spend toward cheap Chinese models, current Street profit forecasts for US AI infrastructure players could prove to be a fraction of consensus — a direct margin/valuation risk to watch in earnings.

insights.claim: Pento believes AI is a genuine productivity technology that will pay off over years and decades, similar to the internet, but says the current AI investment bubble is 'leaps and bounds' larger than the dot-com bubble was.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Separates the long-run technology thesis (bullish) from the near-term financial-market thesis (bearish) — useful framing for distinguishing AI adoption optimism from AI-stock valuation risk.
insights.quote: this is an investment bubble that's you know leaps and bounds ahead of what we saw in the internet bubble

insights.claim: Pento argues long-duration AI-linked corporate debt is mispriced: he cites SpaceX issuing very long-dated bonds only ~100-150 basis points above Treasuries, arguing that given uncertain multi-decade inflation and unproven long-term productivity payoff from the technology, such tight spreads don't compensate for the risk — and that rising borrowing costs generally will pressure the cash-flow economics of AI-related debt issuance broadly.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Flags long-duration AI-adjacent credit as a specific mispricing to watch — spreads that don't reflect multi-decade technology and inflation uncertainty are vulnerable to repricing wider.
insights.quote: no one has any earthly idea what condition the inflation environment will be in 50 years

insights.claim: Pento agrees that if his deflationary-depression scenario unfolds, the availability of capital for AI buildout will simply dry up, compounding the physical-world constraints (power, land, water, skilled labor) other guests have raised as limits on how many data centers can actually get built.
insights.speaker: Michael Pento
insights.so_what: Adds a capital-availability constraint on top of physical bottlenecks as a reason current data-center buildout projections may prove overstated if a credit crunch hits.
